analysis.answer: Current law allows landlords to raise rent by any amount provided they give 60 days' written notice. This measure explicitly restricts rent increases to a maximum of 5 percent in any 12-month period, while maintaining an exemption for newer housing units that were first occupied within the last 15 years.

Renters residing in units older than 15 years benefit from capped rent increases and enhanced financial predictability. Landlords and property owners of those same units bear the cost of limited revenue potential, which may be particularly impactful during periods of high inflation.

Landlords may respond by routinely increasing rent by the maximum allowed 5 percent each year to avoid falling behind market rates, whereas previously they might have left rent flat for longer periods. Some property owners might reduce maintenance spending to offset revenue limits, or attempt to convert rental units into ownership units (condos). Because of the 15-year rolling exemption, developers maintain an incentive to build new rental housing.

The measure addresses the problem of sudden, large rent spikes that can displace tenants and cause housing instability. The mechanism is a hard cap on annual rent growth for older units. By explicitly exempting new construction for 15 years, it attempts to avoid the perverse incentive of discouraging the creation of new housing supply that often accompanies strict price controls.
Existing tenants in older units gain leverage and security against large price increases. Landlords lose pricing discretion and power over those properties.

The broader economic effects of rent control policies are actively disputed. Many economists find that while rent caps provide immediate stability for incumbent tenants, they reduce the overall quantity and quality of available rental housing over time, misallocate units, and can drive up rents in unregulated sectors of the market. Proponents, however, argue that capping increases (particularly with rolling exemptions for new construction) effectively prevents tenant displacement and homelessness without significantly dampening new housing supply.
